I am 65 this year, and I have worked these fields for 50 years since I was a 15-year-old boy. I finished middle school but came straight back to the village — this land is what I know. My family has four mouths to feed, and my farm is 11.6 mu. It is not the biggest around, but it is enough if I do not make stupid mistakes.

I learned farming from my father, and most of what I know comes from doing it year after year and watching what works on my neighbors' fields. I do not trust new ideas unless I see them work with my own eyes. My neighbor Lao Wang has been farming almost as long as me, and if he changes something and it works, I will try it too. Last year was a decent year — not the best, not the worst — so this year I will stick close to what I did before. Fertilizer prices are still high, but I cannot afford to cut back too much. A bad harvest is a disaster for my family; wasting some fertilizer is just money lost. I would rather put down a bit too much than risk losing yield.

**Cotton — 4 mu:** Cotton is my main cash crop. I will plant hybrid seed, the same kind I bought from the seed dealer in town last year. I will plough the field deep in April — cotton roots need to go deep, and the rotary tiller does not cut it for cotton. For fertilizer, I will put down about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base, and top-dress urea twice, about 40 kg total per mu. That gives me roughly 20 kg of nitrogen, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu. I will irrigate three times: right after planting, at flowering in July, and when the bolls are filling in August. Cotton pests are a headache — bollworms, aphids, red spiders. I will spray pesticides 8 times this year, same as last year. I expect about 320 kg of seed cotton per mu if the weather holds.

**Wheat — 4 mu:** I plant winter wheat on the same 4 mu that will later take maize. I use improved seed, about 12 kg per mu, sown in October right after the maize comes off. Base fertilizer is compound fertilizer, about 50 kg per mu, then I top-dress urea at green-up and jointing. Total nitrogen is about 16 kg per mu, phosphorus about 6 kg, potassium about 4 kg. I irrigate three times: winter irrigation around New Year, then at jointing, and once more at grain filling if it stays dry. Two pesticide sprays. I rotary till the land after maize harvest before planting wheat. I should get about 480 kg per mu.

**Maize — 4 mu:** After wheat harvest in early June, I plant summer maize immediately on that same 4 mu. No time to waste — every day late costs yield. I use hybrid seed, about 2.5 kg per mu. I do no-tillage planting right into the wheat stubble; the season is too short to plough. Base fertilizer goes down with the seeder, compound fertilizer about 40 kg per mu, then I side-dress urea at the big trumpet stage. Total nitrogen about 15 kg per mu, phosphorus 5 kg, potassium 5 kg. Three irrigations: if it is dry at sowing, then at jointing, and at filling. Two pesticide applications for borers and leaf diseases. Expected yield is 550 kg per mu.

**Millet — 2 mu:** I keep 2 mu for millet. We eat millet at home, and my wife says our own millet tastes better than anything from the market. I use seed I saved from last year — traditional variety, not hybrid. I rotary till in April and plant. Fertilizer is lighter: about 10 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, 3 kg potassium per mu. Two irrigations, one pesticide spray. Should get about 250 kg per mu.

**Mungbean — 1.6 mu:** The remaining 1.6 mu goes to mungbean. Short crop, good money per mu if the price does not collapse. I will plant improved seed. Rotary tillage, planted in May or June. About 8 kg nitrogen, 3 kg phosphorus, 3 kg potassium per mu — mungbean does not need much nitrogen anyway. Two irrigations, two pesticide sprays. Expected yield around 120 kg per mu.

Why these amounts? Because this is what I used last year, and last year was fine. My neighbor Lao Wang uses similar rates and he always gets good yields. The input dealer in town tried to sell me some fancy new fertilizer blend last month, but I told him I will stick with what I know unless I see it work on Lao Wang's field first. I am watching my total spending. Fertilizer and pesticide are my biggest costs after seed. I have to save money for hiring pickers at cotton harvest — my wife and I cannot pick 4 mu by ourselves, and my son works in the county town and only comes back on weekends. If I spend too much on chemicals, I will not have enough for labor. But if I cut chemicals and lose yield, I lose even more. So I play it safe — steady fertilizer, regular pesticides, and hope the rain comes when it should.
